name: Northern Guiyang Hmong
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Northern Guiyang Hmong is not in the catalog. The only stress-keyword title Glottolog attaches to it, Kan Hua (1980) on voiced/voiceless initials in Amdo Tibetan vs stressed/unstressed syllables in Old Tibetan, is a false link: the Glottolog reference page states the languoid was a 'computerized assignment from \"zhuo\"' out of LaPolla's Tibeto-Burman bibliography. It is about a Tibeto-Burman language, priority none. No first-hand statement on word stress in Northern Guiyang Hmong was found in any open source: the ISO 639-3 change request (downloaded) names the descriptive sources (Wang Fushi 1985 Miaoyu jianzhi; Wang & Mao 1995), none online; Ratliff 2010 (sealang) is a 404; A Speech Prosody 2012 paper on Mo Piu tone (a variety only tentatively assigned to Guiyang Miao, subdialect unspecified) was downloaded and is silent on stress. Files with.

sources.citation: 王辅世 Wang Fushi (ed.). 1985. 苗语简志 [A sketch of the Miao language]. Beijing: Minzu chubanshe. (full scan, archive.org/details/20220317_20220317_1109)
sources.note: Nothing for this variety. The book's phonology chapter treats Dananshan (Chuanqiandian proper) with sketches of Layiping and Yanghao; the Guiyang subdialect appears only in the distribution list (p.104: 北部土语 ~60,000 speakers, Guiyang city outskirts, Pingba Linka, Qianxi, Jinsha, Zhenning, Kaiyang, Xiuwen, Guiding) and as the comparison point 摆托 Baituo, Qingyan, Guiyang (p.135 '摆托 (贵阳次方言的代表点, 在贵阳市青岩)'; p.140) in the lexical/grammatical comparison. scanned has 0 hits for 重音/轻读/重读/轻重; the only 轻声 remark (p.12) concerns Xiangxi (Layiping) prefixes. Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Purnell, Herbert C. (ed.). 1972. Miao and Yao linguistic studies: selected articles in Chinese (transl. Chang Yü-hung & Chu Kwo-ray). Data Paper 88. Ithaca: Cornell SEAP. sources.note: Pai t'o (摆托), Ch'ing yen, Kweiyang City is datapoint 5 'Kweiyang subdialect' (p.56 fn.1) in 'Chinese loanwords in Miao', with tone-numbered Pai t'o forms in the loan charts; the 'brief description' says the Kweiyang subdialect has three subdivisions. The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the volume. Silent.

sources.citation: Caelen-Haumont, Geneviève & Katarina Bartkova. 2013. Manual and automatic tone annotation: the case of an endangered language from North Vietnam "Mo Piu". Proceedings of Interspeech 2013 (Lyon, 25-29 Aug.), 1448-1452. doi:10.21437/interspeech.2013-377 (HAL hal-00947394; ISCA Archive interspeech_2013/caelenhaumont13_interspeech).
sources.note: Instrumental (F0 in semi-tones, 5-level scale) tone annotation of an 8-category Hmong-Mien prototone word list (after Ratliff) recorded by two Mo Piu speakers, of whom only one speaker's data are analysed here: 206 (often compound) words x 3 repetitions = 818 vowel/tone tokens, restricted to 525 vowels of the strict prototone list; annotated with MISTRAL+ (semi-automatic) and PROSOTRAN (automatic). Both systems find mostly falling (68%/55%) and level (30%/43%) patterns, rising only ~2%, ~70% agreement on slope direction; the tone candidates with the largest populations are /43, 54, 41, 33/ (f…

tone.quote: Concerning the relation between Mo Piu tones and the 8 prototones, in the limits of our data, it is only possible to put forward that the 8 prototones do not lead to 8 Mo Piu tones. A tone restructuring is made in Mo Piu under the pressure of history, internal reorganizationand loan words. Nowadays in Mo Piu, the main tone patterns are falling slopes and plateaux. Some prototones 2, 3, 5, 8 seem to have merged into the same tone /43/, while the prototone 1 seems to mostly correspond to the tone /54/. As for the other prototones, other data are needed to confirm whether 6 is split up in two tones /43, 41/, and whether 4 leads to the plateau /33/.
tone.locator: p. 1451, section 5 'Conclusion', final paragraph (abstract p. 1448: 'The main tone patterns detected in our study are /41, 43, 54/ as falling slopes and /33/ as a plateau.')
tone.summary: Mo Piu (Guiyang-Miao-affiliated variety, N Vietnam): lexical tone language; phonetic study finds four main tone patterns /54/, /43/, /41/ (falling) and /33/ (level), rising ~2%; the 8 Hmong-Mien proto-tone categories do not yield 8 Mo Piu tones (2,3,5,8 apparently merged to /43/, 1 -> /54/); voice quality and tone sandhi not examined.
